  1146→\paragraph{Robertson.}
  1147→Table~\ref{tab:comparison_robertson} and Figure~\ref{fig:robertson_comparison} compare the time-stepping behaviour on the Robertson system ($A \to B$, $2B \to C+B$, $C+B \to A+C$; $k_1 = 0.04$, $k_2 = 3\times10^6$, $k_3 = 1$, $A_0 = 10{,}000$, $B_0 = C_0 = 0$) over $[0, 10^4]$. This system is deterministically stiff ($k_2 \gg k_1, k_3$), but the stochastic initial condition ($B_0 = 0$) shapes how each method experiences that stiffness.
  1148→
  1149→For FP-FSP, the flux-adaptive time step $\delta t = \varepsilon_{\Delta t}/\Phi_{\mathrm{total}}$ grows as $A$ is slowly consumed. At $t = 0$, $\Phi_{\mathrm{total}} \approx k_1 A_0 = 400$, giving $\delta t \approx 2.5\times10^{-3}$. As $A$ converts to $C$ over time, $\Phi_{\mathrm{total}} \approx k_1 A(t)$ decreases monotonically and $\delta t$ grows correspondingly, reaching ${\sim}10^2$ near $t_f = 10^4$ (Figure~\ref{fig:robertson_comparison}a). FP-FSP completes the full horizon with a compact state space maintained by flux-based pruning.
  1150→
  1151→For Krylov-FSP-SSA, $\tau$ doubles after every accepted step with zero FSP rejections. Starting from $(A_0, 0, 0)$, the quasi-steady state $B_{\mathrm{ss}} \approx \sqrt{k_1 A / k_2} \approx 0.01 \ll 1$ means the FSP mass is conserved at any $\tau$: the system barely moves in state space and no probability leaves the projection boundary. Accordingly, $\tau$ grows exponentially---0.1, 0.2, 0.4, \ldots---completing $t_f = 10^4$ in 17 steps (${\approx}0.01$\,s). The matrix exponential resolves the fast $k_2 B^2$ timescale internally without exposing it as a step-size constraint.
  1152→
  1153→\begin{table}[!htbp]
  1154→\centering
  1155→\caption{Robertson comparison ($t_f = 10^4$): FP-FSP (flux-adaptive $\delta t$, growing from ${\approx}2.5\times10^{-3}$ to ${\sim}10^2$) vs.\ Krylov-FSP-SSA (Algorithm~2 of~\cite{VoSidje2016}, $\varepsilon=10^{-2}$, $\tau_{\mathrm{init}}=0.1$, $r=1$). Both methods complete $t_f$.}
  1156→\label{tab:comparison_robertson}
  1157→\begin{tabular}{lcc}
  1158→\hline
  1159→Metric & FP-FSP & Krylov-FSP-SSA \\
  1160→\hline
  1161→Wall time (s) & --- & ${<}0.1$ \\
  1162→Steps / Iterations & --- & 17 ($\tau$: $0.1 \to 3{,}447$) \\
  1163→Rejections & --- & 0 \\
  1164→Time reached & $10^4$ (complete) & $10^4$ (complete) \\
  1165→$\delta t$ / $\tau$ range & $2.5\times10^{-3} \to {\sim}10^2$ & $0.1 \to 3{,}447$ \\
  1166→\hline
  1167→\end{tabular}
  1168→\end{table}
  1169→
  1170→\begin{figure}[!htbp]
  1171→    \centering
  1172→    \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{robertson_comparison.pdf}
  1173→    \caption{Robertson system ($t_f = 10^4$): time step vs.\ iteration (log scale). (a) FP-FSP $\delta t$: grows monotonically from ${\approx}2.5\times10^{-3}$ (set by $\Phi_{\mathrm{total}} \approx k_1 A_0 = 400$ at $t{=}0$) to ${\sim}10^2$ near $t_f$ as $A$ is consumed and $\Phi_{\mathrm{total}}$ decreases; the bimolecular states ($B{\geq}2$) in the projection carry negligible probability and therefore negligible flux weight. (b) Krylov-FSP-SSA $\tau$: doubles after each accepted step from $\tau_{\mathrm{init}} = 0.1$ to $\tau \approx 3{,}447$, with zero FSP rejections, completing $t_f = 10^4$ in 17 steps; starting from $B_0{=}0$, the quasi-steady state $B_{\mathrm{ss}} \approx 0.01$ means FSP mass is conserved at any $\tau$.}
  1174→    \label{fig:robertson_comparison}
  1175→\end{figure}
  1176→
  1177→\paragraph{Summary.}
  1178→The comparison reveals clearly complementary strengths rooted in different algorithmic choices about step-size control and pruning. On the oscillatory Oregonator, flux-adaptive time stepping provides a decisive advantage: FP-FSP scales $\delta t$ to the instantaneous activity level and maintains a compact state space via flux-based pruning, while Krylov-FSP-SSA is locked at $\tau \approx 10^{-6}$ by mass-conservation failures and cannot complete $t_f = 0.11$. On the bottleneck system, FP-FSP with a fixed step $\delta t = 1/k_2 = 10$\,s keeps the depth-1 expansion pace-matched with the probability wavefront; Krylov-FSP-SSA's exponentially growing $\tau$ produces a 14-state projection that underestimates $\langle C \rangle$ by 40$\times$, with no FSP rejection signal because the missing-row truncation does not reduce $\sum w$ within the truncated system. On Robertson, both methods complete $t_f = 10^4$: FP-FSP's probability-weighted flux $\Phi_{\mathrm{total}} \approx k_1 A(t)$ decreases as $A$ is consumed, allowing $\delta t$ to grow smoothly from ${\approx}2.5\times10^{-3}$ to ${\sim}10^2$; Krylov-FSP-SSA exploits the quasi-steady $B_{\mathrm{ss}} \approx 0.01$ to double $\tau$ freely, finishing in just 17 steps.
  1179→
  1180→\subsection{Efficiency Under Corrected Krylov-FSP-SSA Parameters}
  1181→\label{subsec:corrected_efficiency}
  1182→
  1183→A natural question is whether the efficiency advantages in Tables~\ref{tab:comparison_oregonator}--\ref{tab:comparison_robertson} hold when Krylov-FSP-SSA parameters are tuned to produce \emph{correct} results. Table~\ref{tab:corrected_efficiency} summarises this comparison.
  1184→
  1185→\textbf{Oregonator.} The $\tau$-lock at $\tau \approx 10^{-6}$ arises because the Krylov matrix exponential loses mass conservation for any larger step, owing to the large individual propensities ($k_3 X Z \sim 10^5$). This is independent of $\varepsilon$: tighter pruning reduces $|\mathcal{S}|$ but does not lower the propensity of the surviving states. Krylov-FSP-SSA therefore cannot complete $t_f = 0.11$ at any practical efficiency, regardless of parameter tuning.
  1186→
  1187→\textbf{Bottleneck.} We conducted an extensive parameter search on the bottleneck system to determine whether Krylov-FSP-SSA can be tuned to match FP-FSP's accuracy. The distribution of $C$ given $B{=}1$ is not concentrated at $\langle C \rangle \approx 5$: the bottleneck transition $A \to B$ occurs uniformly over $[0, t_f]$, so $C \mid B{=}1$ spreads approximately uniformly from $0$ to $k_2 t_f = 1000$, with mean $\approx 500$. Accurate resolution therefore requires the projection to track the wavefront at $C \approx k_2 t$ throughout the simulation.
  1188→
  1189→The faithful implementation (Algorithm~2 of~\cite{VoSidje2016}) correctly retains $B{=}1$ via the joint probability-and-derivative filter ($\mathtt{droptol} = 10^{-10}$). The remaining failure is a conflict between step-size growth and state-space expansion. After a successful step, $\tau$ is multiplied by the growth factor (default 2); the $r{=}1$ depth expansion adds only one new $C$-state. For the wavefront to stay within the projection, the expansion depth must satisfy $r \gtrsim k_2 \tau$. As $\tau$ grows (100 $\to$ 3{,}700\,s in the default run), $r$ would need to grow proportionally, making the projection cost scale as the product $k_2 \tau_{\max} \times n_{\mathrm{steps}} \approx k_2 t_f = 1000$. Capping $\tau \leq 1/k_2 = 10$\,s forces $\sim$1{,}000 steps (comparable to FP-FSP) but removes the efficiency advantage of large accepted steps. Increasing $r$ at a fixed $\tau$ improves accuracy but raises per-step cost without addressing the $\tau$-growth coupling.
  1190→
  1191→Empirically, tuning $(\varepsilon, \tau, r)$ over a wide range (Table~\ref{tab:corrected_efficiency}) achieves at best $\langle C \rangle \approx 4.72$ ($\sim$5\% error) at comparable wall time to FP-FSP---which achieves ${<}0.1\%$ error under default parameters. The flux-based method avoids this conflict because FP-FSP uses a fixed step $\delta t = 1/k_2 = 10$\,s, and the exit-flux criterion retains wavefront states regardless of their probability because their outgoing flux $k_2 p(B{=}1, C{=}c)$ is large relative to the total system flux.
  1192→
  1193→\textbf{Robertson ($t_f = 10^4$).} Both methods complete $t_f = 10^4$. Krylov-FSP-SSA finishes in 17 steps (${\approx}0.01$\,s), with $\tau$ doubling from 0.1 to ${\approx}3{,}447$ and zero rejections, because starting from $B_0 = 0$, the stiff $k_2 B^2$ dynamics are not triggered in the FSP sense. FP-FSP's probability-weighted flux $\Phi_{\mathrm{total}} \approx k_1 A(t)$ decreases as $A$ is consumed, allowing $\delta t$ to grow from ${\approx}2.5\times10^{-3}$ to ${\sim}10^2$ over the simulation. The step count is therefore much larger than for Krylov-FSP-SSA, but each step is cheap due to the compact, flux-pruned state space. On Robertson, Krylov-FSP-SSA is the more efficient method.
  1194→
  1195→\begin{table}[!htbp]
  1196→\centering
  1197→\caption{Efficiency with corrected Krylov-FSP-SSA parameters. ``Default'' uses the parameters from Figures~\ref{fig:oregonator_comparison}--\ref{fig:robertson_comparison}; ``best tuned'' is the best result over a sweep of $(\varepsilon, \tau, r)$ for each system. Best bottleneck result: $\langle C \rangle \approx 4.72$ (${\sim}5\%$ error) at comparable wall time to FP-FSP ($\langle C \rangle = 4.978$, ${<}0.1\%$ error). FP-FSP times from Tables~\ref{tab:comparison_oregonator}--\ref{tab:comparison_bottleneck}.}
  1198→\label{tab:corrected_efficiency}
  1199→\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
  1200→\hline
  1201→System & FP-FSP & KrylovFSP (default) & KrylovFSP (best tuned) & Verdict \\
  1202→\hline
  1203→Oregonator & 37\,s & 103\,s, 2.7\% & DNF ($\tau$-lock, all $\varepsilon$) & FP-FSP wins \\
  1204→Bottleneck & 1.0\,s & ${<}0.1$\,s, $\langle C\rangle{=}0.12$ (wavefront trunc.) & 0.9\,s, $\langle C\rangle{\approx}4.72$ (${\sim}5\%$ err) & FP-FSP: ${<}0.1\%$ err \\
  1205→Robertson $t_f{=}10^4$ & ---\,s, many steps & ${<}0.1$\,s, 17 iters & --- & Krylov-FSP wins \\
  1206→\hline
  1207→\end{tabular}
  1208→\end{table}
  1209→
  1210→The key findings reveal qualitatively distinct failure modes. On the Oregonator, the Krylov $\tau$-lock is intrinsic to the mass-conservation criterion and cannot be resolved by any parameter choice: large propensities ($k_3 X Z \sim 10^5$) force $\tau \lesssim 10^{-6}$ regardless of $\varepsilon$. On the bottleneck system, the exponential growth of $\tau$ creates a fundamental conflict with depth-$r$ expansion: keeping the projection pace-matched with the wavefront requires $r \gtrsim k_2 \tau$, but $\tau$ grows without bound; the best achievable accuracy is $\sim$5\% error regardless of $(\varepsilon, \tau, r)$. On Robertson, both methods succeed, but with qualitatively different step-size dynamics: FP-FSP's probability-weighted flux control allows $\delta t$ to grow as $A$ is consumed, while Krylov-FSP-SSA's matrix exponential absorbs the stiff $k_2 B^2$ timescale internally, reaching $t_f = 10^4$ in 17 steps. The complementary picture is clear: flux-based methods excel on problems with oscillatory dynamics or connectivity bottlenecks where large propensities at high-probability states or conduit states require careful step-size and pruning control; Krylov methods excel on stiff problems where the stiff timescale is not directly relevant to the dominant distribution, and the matrix exponential can step over it without mass loss.
  1211→
  1212→\section{Discussion}
  1213→\label{sec:discussion}
  1214→
  1215→The numerical results indicate that flux-based pruning can preserve network connectivity across a range of benchmark systems while maintaining competitive compression and accuracy. The comparison with the Krylov-FSP-SSA baseline in Section~\ref{sec:comparison} further demonstrates that the two main contributions---flux-aware pruning and flux-adaptive time stepping---provide complementary robustness advantages on multiscale systems. The method targets two coupled difficulties in adaptive FSP: controlling the loss of important transitions when states are pruned, and selecting time steps that reflect the instantaneous activity level of the system. The flux-based pruning rule protects low-probability states that carry significant probability flow, and the flux-adaptive time-step selection aligns the numerical step size with the dominant rates in the truncated system.
  1216→
  1217→The expansion rule for the proposed method is deliberately simple (fixed $r$-step expansion), and the pruning parameters $(\alpha, \epsilon_{\mathrm{flux}})$ are fixed in time. This suffices for the test problems considered here, but more complicated networks may require additional structure in the adaptation strategy. For example, systems with strong directional drift or localized reaction zones could benefit from combining flux-based criteria with short trajectory bursts \cite{Dinh2016} to identify dynamically relevant regions before committing them to the FSP state space.

1. Primary Request and Intent:
   The user's main requests this session were:
   - Study the `corrected_krylov` branch changes (max flux vs total flux, new `expand!`, `reconstruct_generator`, `expv`)
   - Run `examples/robertson.jl` (FP-FSP) and KrylovFSP on Robertson tf=1e4 and compare

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - **Closed-form vs absorbing-form CME generator**: Closed form has diagonal = only outflow to states IN S (mass-conserving). Absorbing form has diagonal = total outflow from each state (probability leaks out to sink when hitting boundary). KrylovFSP's FSP mass-loss criterion requires absorbing form.
   - **Maximum flux vs total flux dt formula**: `dt = ε_dt / maximum(out_flux)` (Robertson, old Pluto notebook style) vs `dt = ε_dt / sum(out_flux)` (other systems). Actual per-step dt peaks at ~0.026 for Robertson, NOT ~10².
   - **Robertson system dynamics**: With k₁=0.04, k₂=3×10⁶, k₃=1, A₀=10000; true A(tf=10⁴)≈507, C≈9493. State space peaks at ~2400 states, settles to ~442 at tf.
   - **KrylovFSP τ-lock**: With closed generator, FSP criterion never triggered (mass always ≈1), τ doubles to 3447, |S|=4, C=16 (wrong). With absorbing generator, τ correctly locks at ~10⁻³ due to k₂ stiffness, reaching only t=24 (0.24% of tf).

3. Files and Code Sections:

   - **`src/generator.jl`** (MODIFIED — critical fix):
     Added `absorbing::Bool=false` keyword to `build_generator`. When `absorbing=true`, diagonal includes ALL outgoing propensities regardless of whether destination is in S:
     ```julia
     function build_generator(sp::StateSpace{E,T}, model, rates, t::Real;
                              absorbing::Bool=false) where {E,T}
         ...
         @inbounds for j in 1:n
             x = sp.states[j]
             col_sum = zero(T)
             for k in 1:n_rxn
                 α = convert(T, model.propensities[k](x, rates, t))
                 α > 0 || continue
                 y = x + model.stoichvecs[k]
                 i = get(sp.index, y, 0)
                 if i != 0
                     push!(I, i); push!(J, j); push!(V, α)
                 end
                 if absorbing || i != 0
                     col_sum += α
                 end
             end
             if col_sum > 0
                 push!(I, j); push!(J, j); push!(V, -col_sum)
             end
         end
         ...
     end
     ```

   - **`src/adaptive_fsp/krylov_fsp.jl`** (MODIFIED — two changes):
     1. Removed `mode=:error_estimate` (invalid for non-Hermitian):
        ```julia
        # Before:
        p_new = expv(τ_step, A, sp.probs; mode=:error_estimate, tol=alg.Tol)
        # After:
        p_new = expv(τ_step, A, sp.probs; tol=alg.Tol)
        ```
     2. Changed to absorbing generator:
        ```julia
        # Before:
        A, _, _ = build_generator(sp, model, rates, t)
        # After:
        A, _, _ = build_generator(sp, model, rates, t; absorbing=true)
        ```

   - **`src/adaptive_fsp/solve.jl`** (read, key change from user's commit):

     - Uses `expv` from ExponentialUtilities instead of `expmv` from Expokit
     - Line 107: `total_flux = maximum(out_flux)`

   - **`paper/ex_article.tex`** (read, needs full Robertson section rewrite):
     Current Robertson section (lines 1146–1210) contains:
     - Wrong dt claim: "reaching ~10²" (actual peak: 0.026)
     - Wrong KrylovFSP description: "17 steps, completes tf" (actual with absorbing: τ-locked, t=24)

     All these need to be updated with the correct values from the simulation.
